results.key_finding: First-line treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 5 days). High-efficacy DMTs (natalizumab, fingolimod, or anti-CD20 therapies) are often preferred given the aggressive initial presentation.

output.summary: Tumefactive MS is a rare presentation of demyelinating disease characterized by large (>2 cm) lesions that mimic brain tumors. Diagnosis often requires brain biopsy when imaging and CSF findings are inconclusive. MRI features favoring demyelination over neoplasm include open ring enhancement, DWI shine-through without restriction, and MR spectroscopy showing elevated myo-inositol without lipid peaks. Acute treatment with high-dose IV corticosteroids has been used, with plasma exchange as an alternative in refractory cases. Approximately 70% of patients with tumefactive demyelination go on to develop clinically definite relapsing-remitting MS.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start natalizumab in a JC virus-antibody-positive patient (especially with high index) without explicit benefit-risk discussion of PML
Do not initiate fingolimod without a baseline ECG and first-dose bradyarrhythmia monitoring; avoid in patients with second-degree AV block, prior MI, or severe sleep apnea
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as a maintenance treatment for MS — they are ineffective long-term and carry significant harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal-cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS criteria — cord lesions change relapse counting and management

Do not pursue aggressive cytoreductive surgery for a presumed tumefactive demyelinating lesion before exhausting non-invasive workup — open ring enhancement, CSF OCBs, and AQP4/MOG serology should be obtained first

Exclude NMOSD and MOGAD with AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG cell-based assays before committing to an MS diagnosis and DMT

key_clinical_evidence: MS is a clinical-radiographic diagnosis: the 2024 revised McDonald requires dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) plus exclusion of better explanations — no single test confirms it

MS-typical MRI regions are periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, and spinal cord — recognising a lesion in three of these regions establishes DIS for an attack-meeting clinical event

CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands (≥2 bands not present in paired serum) can substitute for DIT under the 2024 revised McDonald when DIS is met — this changes the calculus for clinically isolated syndromes

Short-segment (<2 vertebral bodies), peripheral, dorsolateral or dorsal-column spinal cord lesions strongly favour MS over NMOSD (which characteristically produces longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis ≥3 segments)

Tumefactive demyelinating lesions are a recognised MS variant — distinguishing imaging features from neoplasm include open ring enhancement, prominent intralesional venules, less mass effect than expected for size, and CSF OCBs; brain biopsy should be a last resort
Open-ring enhancement with the opening oriented toward the cortex is a high-specificity sign of demyelination, distinguishing tumefactive MS from neoplasm and abscess
AQP4-IgG and MOG-IgG must be ordered as cell-based assays, not ELISA — the older ELISA-based AQP4 assays have unacceptable false-negative rates
T1 hypointense 'black holes' indicate axonal loss from prior inflammatory episodes and contribute evidence of dissemination in time even without simultaneous enhancing lesions

Choice of DMT — platform agent (interferon-β, glatiramer, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate) vs. high-efficacy agent (natalizumab, ocrelizumab, ofatumumab, cladribine, S1P modulators) — should weigh disease activity, MRI burden, patient comorbidities, JCV serostatus, and reproductive plans
If the initial brain MRI does not include the spinal cord, extending imaging to cervical and thoracic cord is essential — both for diagnostic DIS and for relapse counting

Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: McDonald 2024: dissemination in space and time is established on MRI, and oligoclonal bands substitute for dissemination in time rather than being required — the reviewers' point.

July 2026 review applied end to end: brain and cervical/thoracic cord MRI use an MS protocol; CSF is conditional, never mandatory; OCT/VEP and AQP4/MOG testing answer selected optic or atypical questions rather than forming a blanket panel.

The 2024 revised McDonald framework recognizes the optic nerve as a fifth topography and accepts the kappa free-light-chain index as an alternative positive-CSF marker; these additions do not make optic testing or lumbar puncture universal.

mri.impression: Large expansile right hemispheric white matter lesion (4.2 cm) with surrounding edema and incomplete ring enhancement, with the open portion facing the cortex — findings suspicious for an underlying mass or primary brain neoplasm, though the open ring enhancement pattern raises the possibility of tumefactive demyelination. Diffuse confluent T2/FLAIR signal abnormalities involving the midbrain, pons, middle cerebellar peduncles, right pontomedullary junction, right anterior cerebellum, splenium of the corpus callosum, right thalamus, and posterior basal ganglia, with patchy enhancement. No evidence of restricted diffusion to suggest abscess or acute infarction. MR angiography normal — no evidence of vasculitis. The extensive, multifocal involvement crossing vascular territories, combined with the open ring enhancement pattern, is atypical for a single neoplastic process and should prompt consideration of tumefactive demyelinating disease, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM), or less likely, CNS lymphoma

CSF oligoclonal bands are present in approximately 85-95% of MS but are typically absent in ADEM — their presence in a tumefactive lesion context strongly favors MS over ADEM

The DWI shine-through phenomenon (high signal on DWI but normal or elevated ADC) reflects T2 prolongation rather than true restricted diffusion, and is an important distinguishing feature from brain abscess

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. James Kowalczyk is a 29-year-old right-handed Caucasian man with no significant past medical history who was brought to the emergency department after a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Per the patient's roommate, the patient awoke that morning complaining of a severe right frontotemporal headache, described as the worst headache of his life, and shortly thereafter collapsed with generalized shaking of all four extremities lasting approximately 90 seconds. Emergency medical services administered intravenous midazolam 5 mg en route to the hospital, after which the seizure activity ceased. In the emergency department, naloxone was empirically administered given uncertain circumstances, with no response, and the patient received intravenous normal saline for volume resuscitation. On further history-taking from family members, they report that over the preceding six weeks, the patient has experienced progressive left-sided weakness, initially noticed as difficulty using his left hand for typing at work, then progressing to left leg heaviness and an unsteady gait. Family also reports that the patient has become increasingly lethargic over the past several months, sleeping 12 to 14 hours per day on weekends, and that his personality has changed with increased impulsivity and irritability, which they initially attributed to work-related stress. Most alarmingly, family estimates the patient has lost approximately 30 to 45 pounds over the past six months without intentional dieting or changes in appetite, though the patient himself seems unconcerned about this. Approximately three weeks prior to presentation, the patient had an upper respiratory tract infection with cough and low-grade fevers lasting about one week, which resolved without medical attention. The family history is notable for the patient's father having been diagnosed with Behcet's disease, prompting early rheumatologic consultation during this admission, though no uveitis, oral ulcers, genital ulcers, or other classic features of Behcet's disease were identified on examination. The patient denies any recent travel, tick exposures, or new sexual contacts. He denies any prior episodes of visual symptoms, limb numbness, or urinary difficulties.
